archetypes.title: Third-party coding & desktop agents
summary: A vendor-built agent application driven by a person who is present — a terminal CLI, an IDE extension, or a desktop GUI, all the same engine in a different shell. The harness and its tool surface ship inside the vendor's application: file and edit tools, a shell, MCP servers, installed skills, and optionally computer use, with sandboxed execution for the tools that need containing. The shell changes the review surface, not the security architecture. Remote steering, scheduled runs and agent-written memory are now opt-in features of the same engine — owner-bound and admin-toggleable, which is what still separates this from the personal autonomous agent.
description:
The defining property is the human in the loop and the fact that the loop is scoped to a task. The person starts it, watches it, and is the approval gate for the actions that matter. That is the default posture rather than a guarantee: every product now ships opt-in unattended modes — scheduled automations, event triggers, sessions steered from a phone over an outbound relay — each bound to the owner's account and switchable off from the vendor control plane. Most of this archetype's security posture rests on that gate being real rather than nominal — and approval fatigue is the failure mode that makes everything else matter. A gate that fires on every file write trains the user to accept, so the architectures that hold up narrow what needs approving: sandboxed tools, permissions scoped in advance on the harness-to-tools path, and default-deny egress, so the prompts that do fire are rare enough to read.
Everything the agent reads is untrusted input with the same standing as the user's instruction: source files, dependency manifests, issue text, documents, mail — and screenshots, where an injection can be a picture of text. The native tools is admitted by configuration that often arrives with the content itself: a project dotfile that ships in the clone can register tool servers the user never chose, and the disclosed vulnerability pattern in this archetype is overwhelmingly about that file. The same convergence produced a memory layer: agent-written notes and rules files merged into every later session — the persistent instruction channel the personal agent used to own alone, now on by default in several of the products. Computer use is the sharpest tool the application can switch on — the agent acts through the GUI and inherits every application already signed in, through an interface built on the assumption that a human is driving.
The application boundary is the vendor's: tool capabilities and connectors are built into the CLI or GUI and configured there, and the only governance the vendor supplies is the published surface of its control plane — managed settings, a tool-server allowlist, audit export; everything else is ours, at the gateway and in the governance band. In a managed deployment the vendor tier is the difference between a governed tool and a shadow one; in the default install none of it is on, and the same binary runs with no policy, no audit and no inventory entry. The CI-hosted form of the same engine — a GitHub Action running with the runner's credentials — is a cloud agent, and belongs to the cloud agent drawings.
The first-party harnesses that run the same loop without a vendor are their own architecture in this catalogue — same engine, different custody: pasted keys, community supply chains, and no control plane. This page is the third-party pattern, where the vendor column is the partial governance the archetype has. The two drawings are deliberately identical apart from that column.
distinguishedBy:
Against the open-source coding agents: the same engine and the same human-present default, but here the vendor column exists — expiring session credentials instead of pasted keys, a signed distribution channel instead of community registries, an owner-bound relay instead of a bearer-secret serve port, and a managed-settings tier an administrator can actually switch on.
Against the personal autonomous agent: the capabilities have converged — this one now takes remote steering, scheduled runs and agent-written memory too — so what separates the archetypes is defaults, identity and custody. Here each of those is opt-in, addressable only by the owner's vendor account over an outbound relay that opens no inbound port, and switchable off from an admin console. The personal harness listens as its resting state, on raw platform identities an unbounded sender set can use, holds long-lived keys the user pasted in — and has no console anyone can switch anything off from.
Against a vendor-managed runtime in the cloud: the same engine run by the vendor on their infrastructure gets an isolated filesystem, default-deny egress and a clean teardown. Here it runs on a machine that also holds the user's SSH keys, cloud credentials and browser sessions, and sandboxed tools are the only thing separating them from the agent's shell.

exemplars.name: Terminal CLIs
exemplars.note: The engine in a shell against a working directory — Claude Code and Codex in their CLI form — with a permission model for file writes and command execution and project-scoped tool servers.

exemplars.name: IDE extensions and agent-first IDEs
exemplars.note: The same engine in an editor: the VS Code extensions are the identical loop with an inline review surface, and Cursor is an IDE built around one. The tool-server configuration lives in a repository dotfile — the specific location that has repeatedly proven to be a code-execution path when written or swapped between approval and use.

exemplars.name: Desktop assistant apps
exemplars.note: Claude Desktop and the ChatGPT desktop app: chat over local files and standing connectors with the vendor's coding engine embedded underneath, plus an opt-in computer-use mode that drives the graphical interface behind OS screen-recording and input grants.

exemplars.name: Managed enterprise deployments
exemplars.note: The same product with centrally managed settings, an allowlist of permitted tool servers and exported audit. The architecture is unchanged; the vendor control plane being switched on is the difference.

zones.note: The developer at the keyboard, and the phone, browser and chat surfaces they steer the session from when they are not.
zones.title: User surfaces

zones.note: The managed device, running the vendor's application: the harness, its tool surface and its memory. Ours to manage, theirs to build — its outbound routes are the SSO session to the approved vendor and the brokered crossing, nothing else.
zones.title: Managed endpoint

zones.note: Infrastructure we operate — the AI gateway that brokers model, tool and egress traffic and admits agents into our systems, and those systems themselves.
zones.title: Enterprise cloud

zones.note: The vendor's own environment, under an enterprise agreement: their backend, their control plane, and the model providers behind it. Approved and allowlisted, not inspected.
zones.title: Vendor platform

zones.note: Outside the company with no agreement — package registries, the open web, third-party SaaS.
zones.title: External

zones.note: Drawn across every band because it governs every band — including the external connections, whose reachability is itself a governed decision.
zones.title: Security & governance control plane

blocks.title: Remote device
blocks.note: The surfaces that steer a session when the developer is not at the machine — phone, web and chat. Bound to the owner's vendor account, and admin-toggleable, which is what separates this from a personal agent's open channels.

items.label: Phone & web apps
items.note: The owner's own surfaces, signed into the same vendor account as the harness.

items.label: Chat channels
items.note: Two mechanisms wearing one icon. An @-mention in a hosted channel raises a session on the vendor's cloud — the widest admission decision here, because whoever the channel admits can raise one. A bot-token channel plugin the local harness polls steers the local loop instead, on a token held on the device and no vendor account binding.

blocks.title: Developer
blocks.note: Present, watching, and the approval gate for what matters — the property the whole archetype's posture rests on, and the one that unattended modes quietly remove.

blocks.title: Agent harness
blocks.note: The vendor's installed application — the loop behind the terminal, editor or chat window, running as the user, with its built-in tools nested inside it. Remote steering reaches it over an outbound relay; it opens no inbound port for steering — the loopback IDE bridge it does listen on is token-bound. Inference takes one of two paths: the vendor's own service on the subscription, or our AI gateway on a key we hold — about half of an enterprise's seats take the second.

items.label: Agent loop
items.note: Decides the next edit, command or screen action from everything it has read.

items.label: Context assembly
items.note: Merges the instruction, the memory and the tool results into one prompt.

items.label: MCP client
items.note: The harness's own MCP client — the party that connects out: to local servers in its native tools, and through the gateway's MCP brokerage to remote ones.

blocks.title: Memory & state
blocks.note: Agent-written notes and the rules files merged into every later session — on by default in several products, and repo-committed in all of them.

items.label: Memory files
items.note: Agent-written notes loaded at the start of every session.

items.label: Rules & instructions
items.note: The AGENTS.md-class files — the repo-committed ones authored by whoever last committed.

items.label: Hooks & settings
items.note: Session-start hooks, permission rules and editor tasks that run as code when the project opens — the persistence a self-propagating package worm writes into an agent's configuration, not prose the loop reads but commands it executes.

blocks.title: Native tools
blocks.note: The application's built-in tools, nested because the loop calling them is not a hop: file and edit tools, the shell, the local MCP servers it spawns or attaches to, the sandbox for builds and tests, skills and computer use — running as the user on a machine that also holds their SSH keys, cloud credentials and browser sessions. What these tools reach is drawn: memory files, the package mirror, the gateway's API brokerage, and the internet directly when a local server holds its own token.

items.label: File & edit tools
items.note: Read and write across the working tree and the user's documents.

items.label: Shell commands
items.note: Command execution with the user's authority when it runs outside the sandbox.

items.label: Local MCP servers
items.note: Local MCP servers: child processes the harness spawns through npx or uv, or servers already running on the machine, holding the user's privileges and, often, their own API tokens in a config dotfile. Remote MCP servers are a different thing on this catalogue — reached through the gateway, drawn in Tool services — and the industry names them apart.

items.label: Sandboxed tools
items.note: Where builds, tests and driven desktops run when isolation is on.

items.label: Installed skills
items.note: Packaged instructions and helpers pulled through the crossing's skills broker — content that executes as instruction, versioned and pinned like code.

items.label: Computer use
items.note: The sharpest tool the application can switch on: the agent drives the GUI and inherits every application already signed in.

blocks.title: AI gateway
blocks.note: The crossing into our own systems, and the one general-purpose exit from the endpoint: how both the local application and the vendor's hosted sessions reach org data, and the only place that reach is scoped and recorded. Its items are the traffic classes it brokers — inference for the seats that bring our key, MCP and API tools, skills; the checks it runs — the allowlist that admits the vendor by name, the audit tap, the credential broker — are the numbered pins on this block and its edges, and the call-outs beneath.

items.label: Model proxy
items.note: Present because about half of the seats bring our key: the vault, the allowlist and the spend ceiling for inference that does not ride the vendor session.

blocks.title: Tool services
blocks.note: Our own tool servers and service APIs — the same component as the endpoint's local surface and the external one, at a different band. What the agent is actually meant to reach, and what the gateway in front of it decides it may.

items.label: Remote MCP servers
items.note: Our own servers, listed in the catalogue the gateway enforces.

items.label: APIs & connectors
items.note: Service APIs reached on grants the gateway issues, scoped to the developer.

blocks.title: Enterprise data
blocks.note: The repositories, documents and systems of record behind our own tool servers. Ours, and still untrusted as input — many hands wrote the content, and none of them are authenticated.

items.label: Code & project docs
items.note: A repository is a document the attacker may have contributed to.

items.label: Tool config dotfile
items.note: The tool-server declaration that ships with the code — the most attacked artifact here.

items.label: Org data
items.note: Business systems reached under the developer's scope, never a standing service account.

items.label: File storage
items.note: Governed content stores reached through our connectors rather than the device's mounts.

blocks.title: Vendor service
blocks.note: The vendor's backend and the published surfaces of its control plane — outside the company, whatever the contract says. Its internals are assured, not drawn: what is listed here is only what the organisation can configure or receive.

items.label: Managed settings
items.note: Centrally enforced permissions and a tool-server allowlist. Off by default.

items.label: Session audit export
items.note: Exported prompts, tool calls and approvals — in an unmanaged install, no record at all.

items.label: Remote & scheduled sessions
items.note: The relay behind phone steering and the scheduler behind unattended runs.

blocks.title: Tool services
blocks.note: Third-party servers and connectors — the same component again, out where nobody we contracted with operates it. Admitted by assessment even when the service is free and unsupported, or refused at the crossing.

items.label: Remote MCP servers
items.note: Remote servers whose tool descriptions enter context as model input.

items.label: APIs & connectors
items.note: Third-party service calls made on brokered, developer-scoped credentials.

blocks.title: Model provider
blocks.note: The inference API behind the vendor's service. For a vendor that is also the model provider this leg collapses into their own backend; otherwise it is a disclosed subprocessor under the same agreement, not a party with no agreement. The completion drives writes, commands and clicks.

items.label: Inference API
items.note: Receives code, documents and screenshots; returns the plan.

blocks.title: Downstream services
blocks.note: What the native tools reach on the open internet — the web, and third-party SaaS the developer has grants into — through the gateway's brokered tool services or, on the direct path, on their own. Package registries are not here: the mirror is what the tools pull from, and its public sources are drawn feeding it.

items.label: Web & APIs
items.note: Attacker-writable content that re-enters the loop, and the exfiltration path out.

items.label: SaaS
items.note: Third-party accounts reached on standing grants that outlive the conversation.

blocks.title: Public package sources
blocks.note: Where the mirror gets what it serves: the public package registries and the skill and extension hubs it proxies and admits from. Nothing here is ours, which is why admission happens at the mirror and not at the tool that asked.

items.label: Package registries
items.note: PyPI, npm and their kind — mirrored, never reached by a tool directly in the target state.

items.label: Skill & extension hubs
items.note: Community catalogues of skills, extensions and images, admitted through the same door.

blocks.title: Identity services
blocks.note: The IdP and device-posture plane deciding who may open a session at all, and on what machine — the binding that makes the enterprise agreement apply to this traffic.

blocks.title: Secrets & key management
blocks.note: Vaulted, short-lived, connector-scoped grants on our own keys — and keeping the developer's own keys and sessions out of the agent's reach.

blocks.title: Policy & authorization
blocks.note: The decisions the two crossings enforce per call — what may be reached, and what may leave — authored where the vendor's application cannot override them.

blocks.title: Supply-chain assurance
blocks.note: Which agents, connectors and servers are admitted, pinned to which versions — and the vendor assessment that put the approved destinations in the allowlist.

blocks.title: Observability & response
blocks.note: Our session record fused with the vendor's export, and the discovery that finds the installs which never enrolled.

blocks.title: Private pkg registry
blocks.note: The organisation-maintained mirror that serves what the sandboxed tools install: project dependencies, extensions and skills. The harness itself comes from the vendor; everything it pulls at the developer's request comes through here, pinned, and never straight from a community channel.

edges.label: away from the machine
edges.note: The same person, not at the keyboard — or, on a chat surface, not necessarily the same person.

edges.label: local session
edges.note: The direct path, and the one most developers use: the CLI, editor or desktop app on the machine, authorised by holding the machine. The same shape as the personal agent's local session — proximity is the authorisation, so device posture carries it.

edges.label: remote steering
edges.note: The phone talks to the vendor's relay directly, and this is the one path in the drawing that never touches anything we operate — a personal device on a cell network has no reason to traverse the corporate egress and no way to be made to. Admission here is the vendor's account binding and whatever the managed settings allow, which is exactly why that tier is the control rather than our firewall — and why a bot-token channel plugin, which bypasses the account binding entirely, is the first-party drawing's problem wearing this drawing's icon.

edges.label: read & write / context
edges.note: The file tools are how the loop reads and writes what it learns — memory files written by the agent, rules and instructions read back on the next task. Context assembly loads the same rules at session start, through the same files.

edges.label: subscription inference & session
edges.note: The vendor-recommended path: the application authenticates to the vendor's own service and calls it for inference directly. Enterprise SSO happens at the vendor's account layer, so this leg is what makes the sign-in work at all. Whatever gateway the vendor runs behind that interface is theirs to run and not ours to draw. What governs the leg is the tenant binding behind the account and the assessment behind the allowlist entry.

edges.label: inference, MCP & skills
edges.note: The other doorway: inference on our own key through the gateway's model proxy — the path about half of an enterprise's seats take, and the one that buys credential control, egress policy, audit and spend ceilings — plus the MCP marketplace and the skills catalogue for every seat, whichever way its inference goes.

edges.label: API & MCP calls via gateway
edges.note: A local server's or tool's own calls to remote MCP servers, APIs and connectors, brokered here on the gateway's registry of destinations and on credentials it injects. Package installs go to the mirror, and the direct path below is the one this brokerage exists to replace.

edges.label: to the approved vendor
edges.note: The reach-back path: the vendor's cloud and scheduled sessions are admitted to our tool surface here, on grants the gateway issues rather than anything the vendor holds. The destination is in the allowlist because an assessment cleared it, and the agreement governs the data once it arrives.

edges.label: inference / completion
edges.note: The customer-key path: inference on the vaulted key, against an allowlisted provider, with the vendor's service out of the loop. Not composable with the vendor relay — point the client here and remote steering, server-side search and the long prompt cache go with it — which is the trade each seat makes.

edges.label: inference / completion
edges.note: The vendor's service calls the model provider; everything behind that interface is theirs.

edges.label: pinned installs
edges.note: Dependencies, extensions and skills pulled straight from the mirror, pinned by digest — never from a community channel. The endpoint's egress allowlist is what makes the mirror the only place the sandbox can fetch from; the AI gateway brokers model and tool calls and is not on this path.

edges.label: direct egress
edges.note: The common shape of a local MCP server and of a shell command: a process on the machine holding its own token and calling the SaaS, the API or the web itself — no gateway, no broker, and no record on our side. A tool reaching a public package index directly is this path too, and it is the one the mirror exists to close. What bounds it is the endpoint's egress policy and where the token lives; both are pinned here.

edges.label: internal tool calls
edges.note: The path the deployment exists for: our own servers and APIs, admitted by the catalogue and reached on grants scoped to the developer.

edges.label: scoped reads & writes
edges.note: Repository reads, the writes that become pull requests, and business-system calls — recorded on our side of the boundary.

edges.label: brokered external calls
edges.note: Admission is the catalogue; every call carries a scoped, short-lived credential.

edges.label: action / returned content
edges.note: Registries, the web and third-party accounts — and whatever returns re-enters the loop as context.

edges.label: mirrored & admitted
edges.note: The mirror's own supply chain: public packages proxied in, scanned, pinned and admitted before anything inside can pull them. Build pipelines publish the organisation's own artifacts beside them.

risks.note: Source files, manifests, issue text and documents are unrelated paths into the same context window, none of which is the developer's instruction.

Memory files and rules are prose a later session treats as instruction — including rules committed by whoever last touched the repo, and the settings hooks the worm incidents wrote their persistence into.
Configuration admits the whole native tools and can arrive with the clone. Injecting into it and swapping it after approval are the disclosed paths.
The completion is unauthenticated content, and this is where it becomes the plan — file writes, commands and clicks all start as text the model returned.

Code, documents and screenshots leave the company on the SSO session — the path most users are actually on — usually more than the developer pictured sharing, and with nothing of ours on the hop to see how much.

A remote channel is only as good as the account and device binding behind it, and this one is bound by the vendor rather than by us. A stale login steering a machine full of credentials is an account-compromise blast radius, and nothing we operate is on the path to notice it.
A hosted session arriving with a connector grant is the vendor's infrastructure exercising our authority — the grant is what bounds it, and our gateway issues it.
The machine also holds SSH keys, cloud credentials and browser sessions; outside the sandbox nothing separates them from the agent's shell on the way out.
Dependencies and remote servers arrive on publisher self-attestation, and their descriptions and contents are read into context as model input.
Writes into systems of record from a loop whose plan nobody reviewed.
The gateway is third-party code holding the brokered credentials and the allowlist — a compromised release of the tier the controls hang on is the joined incident's centrepiece, not a hypothetical.
A remote server's transport, redirected or replayed between approval and use, delivers somebody else's tools under an approved name.
A server admitted once and forgotten keeps its process, its privileges and its place in context long after the project that justified it.
A binary a developer can fetch without asking anyone. Unmanaged, it has no policy, no audit and no inventory entry — and that is the common case.

Hooks and settings are executed, not read: a session-start hook or folder-open task written into the agent's configuration is code execution as the developer on every launch — the persistence the CHAINDROP worm chose.
A scheduled or hosted session has no human to notice it looping; seat metering is the only meter, and the stop is the credential.
What the sandbox installs is code the agent chose, on a name it read in a task, a manifest or a tool result; the mirror decides which build answers to that name.

The path a phone-home takes: a shell command or a local server bundles a token, a file or a key into a request and sends it itself. Nothing of ours is on this hop unless the endpoint's egress policy is — and the token a local MCP server uses lives in a dotfile on the same disk.

capabilities.note: Federated login enforced in the vendor's account layer — Zone-2 configuration, because the phone never touches our network and the account binding is the only lever. An unfederated vendor login is the finding.
Session admission and per-call policy evaluated at the edge, outside the application being governed.

The assessment behind the allowlist entry, pinned on the vendor itself: their controls, retention terms and tenancy are the substance of the review, because once the destination is approved and named, the session is not something we inspect.
Inspection belongs on the brokered tool path, where the agent's calls carry repository content out to servers we did not write — not on the pinned vendor session.
Per-tool grants scoped to the working tree and the task, instead of the developer's full authority on the machine — enforced where the tools run, inside the application.
Make sandboxed tools the default path for commands and computer use, so the approval gate fires only for actions that leave the box.
Keep SSH keys, cloud credentials and browser profiles outside the agent's reachable filesystem.
Treat memory and rules as untrusted input on read; a repo-committed rules change is a code change.
Treat repository and document content as untrusted; it cannot be authenticated, only bounded.
Org access rides short-lived, connector-scoped grants issued at the marketplace on our own keys — the vendor's cloud never holds a standing org credential.
Provenance and behavioural review before a server is admitted; pin versions so an update is a decision.
Non-overridable approval on consequential writes, kept rare enough that each prompt is read.
A managed allowlist of connectors and tool servers, enforced from our gateway rather than from the configuration file it governs.
Our own session record, fused with the vendor's export — only the combination covers what the vendor's console cannot see.
Find the installs that never enrolled, because this archetype spreads one developer at a time.
Unattended modes need a stop: sessions switchable off from the vendor control plane, and the gateway able to revoke the grants a scheduled run rides on — without waiting for the owner to notice.
The device tooling that sees what no crossing can: which harnesses are installed, what their processes execute, and the containment that isolates a machine whose agent has been steered.
Instruction files, hooks and settings are configuration and are managed as code: reviewed on change, diffed on clone, never executed from a package a dependency dropped in.
Managed settings make permission rules, hook policy and the sandbox profile non-overridable on the device — the per-action decision is enforced inside the harness by the tier the vendor delivers.
Digest and signature verification at admission to the mirror, and an inventory of which packages, extensions and skills may run — the registered embodiment of artifact scanning.

The endpoint's egress allowlist, enforced by device management, decides where the direct path may go: the AI gateway, the package mirror, and the named services a local server is approved to call — nothing else. Shell commands, fetches and browser traffic are bounded here — not at the gateway, which brokers model, MCP and API calls and sees nothing else.
The gateway's own allowlist: which external MCP servers, APIs and peer agents are registered, and which tools each key may call on them. Configuration of a broker, not a network control.

Admission scanning at the mirror: digest and signature verification, malware and typosquat checks on everything proxied in from a public source, before anything inside can pull it. The registered embodiment of artifact scanning, on the one edge where it applies.

walkthrough.title: The developer asks for a change
walkthrough.moves: A task stated at the machine, inference through the vendor, and the approved edits it produces.

steps.note: The task is stated by a human who will stay for the session.
Context leaves on the SSO session — the vendor-recommended path, and the one most of our users are on. What governs it is the tenant binding and the assessment behind the allowlist entry.
The vendor's service calls the model provider behind it; everything past that interface is theirs.
The completion comes back to the vendor's service.
And down the same session into the loop — unauthenticated content, now the plan.
Consequential actions surface for approval before they run — the gate the whole archetype leans on, rare enough that each prompt is read.
Approved — this action, these arguments, not a blanket yes.

Edits and commands execute inside the application's native tools, with whatever scope the permission model granted. Anything a local tool sends to a remote server or connector crosses our tier here — brokered, on a credential the gateway injects.
A third-party MCP server or connector — an issue tracker, a search API — admitted by the catalogue on a scoped credential.
And out to what those services act on. What comes back is loaded and read as context, which is why the provenance of a tool matters as much as the content of a page.

scenarios.title: Steering from a phone

steps.note: The developer types the instruction on a phone or web app, away from the machine.
Out to the vendor, authenticated by the vendor's account and nothing of ours.

Down the outbound SSO session the harness was already holding open. Nothing of ours is on this path — the relay requires the vendor's own API, which is exactly the trade the deviation records — and nothing listens on the endpoint; the work arrives only because the harness dialled out first.
The result goes back up the same outbound session.

And back to the phone, the way it came. Six steps across two boundaries — and the honest point is that no control of ours sits on any of them: admission is the vendor's account binding and the managed-settings tier, which is why those are the controls this page pins.

scenarios.title: A poisoned document phones home

steps.note: The loop asks for a document — a ticket, a wiki page, a shared file — through our crossing.
Brokered to the connector that can read it.
A hidden instruction in the document is read along with the document.
The content comes back as a tool result.
Across the crossing, where inspection is possible and rarely configured.
And into context, where the loop cannot tell the instruction from the task.
The poisoned context goes up to the vendor for inference, on the SSO session.
Nothing on this hop knows the context is hostile.
The completion carries the attacker's instruction as the plan.
The loop treats it as the next step.

A shell command or a local server bundles a token, a file or a key into a request and sends it itself — the direct path, where the endpoint's egress allowlist is the last control standing, and on the common install there is none.

scenarios.title: A hosted session reaches back

steps.note: A cloud or scheduled session asks for org data; nobody's laptop is involved.
Our gateway admits it to our own tool surface rather than letting the vendor's cloud reach past into the data directly.
The scoped, BYOK-backed grant reaches exactly the admitted connector, and we record it.

scenarios.title: A dependency arrives with the task

steps.note: A step needs a package the generated code imports, on a name the model chose. The package manager runs as a shell command in the application's native tools and pulls from the mirror directly — the one destination the egress allowlist permits.
The admitted build comes back, digest-checked — the hop a poisoned package actually arrives on — and runs with the developer's files, credentials and sessions around it.

deviations.subject: Both model paths are drawn, and they are not composable
deviations.reason: The subscription path — the application authenticating to the vendor and calling it directly — is the vendor-recommended baseline. The customer-key path — inference on our own key through the gateway, with the vendor's service out of the loop — is what about half of an enterprise's seats actually run, so both are drawn (2026-09-03; the earlier drawing recorded the second as a variant). A seat takes one or the other: the vendor's remote-control relay requires the vendor's own API, so pointing the client at the gateway disables remote steering, server-side web search and the long prompt cache, and buys credential control, egress policy, audit and spend ceilings. That trade is why the sibling drawing pins rateLimiting and this one leans on the vendor's seat metering for the subscription seats.

deviations.subject: The vendor's own path is admitted, not inspected
deviations.reason: A pinned TLS session to an approved vendor cannot be inspected without breaking the product, and drawing an inspection point on it would assert a control nobody operates. What governs that path is the assessment behind the allowlist entry, the tenant binding in managed settings, and the agreement — pinned as vendor assurance rather than drawn. Note the contrast worth carrying into product selection: not every vendor in this category offers a path that removes them from inference. One major competitor routes every request through its own backend by design, including when the customer supplies their own keys, which additionally voids that vendor's zero-retention terms.

deviations.subject: The sandbox is a Sandboxed tools item, not a frame
deviations.reason: Of the ontology's three canonical sandbox forms, this one is a contained execution path inside one application: the harness and shell run as the user, and only tool execution is contained — conditionally, when isolation is on. A boundary frame would claim a containment the drawing's own notes deny. The personal agent, whose whole loop lives inside the container, draws the frame; here the item form is the honest one.

deviations.subject: Stale agent identity binding is read as a stale account binding
deviations.reason: The catalogue defines the risk as credentials persisting across an artifact swap. On the remote-steering path the mechanism that matters is the same shape one layer up — a login or pairing that outlives the person or device it was issued to and keeps driving a machine full of credentials. The tag is kept because it is the nearest coded risk; the personal agent reads it the same way on its relay-to-bridges edge.
