archetypes.title: UI/low-code managed agent runtime
summary: A vendor platform where non-engineers assemble agents from prompts, connectors and triggers. The agents are real, the authors are not engineers, and there is no code review between an afternoon's work and something that acts on production data.
description:
The builder is a self-service surface, and that is both the product and the problem. A business user can create an agent, grant it connectors, give it a trigger and publish it to colleagues without any of the checkpoints a software delivery pipeline would impose — no pull request, no staged rollout, no security sign-off unless the platform enforces one. The result is a population problem rather than an instance problem: individual agents are simple; the risk is four hundred of them, each with connector grants, each authored by someone who has left — and, until somebody actually queries the platform's inventory, no list of which reach customer data. The unmanaged default has no list; the target state queries one.
Credential inheritance is the specific technical trap. A low-code agent typically runs on connections authorised by its author, so a published agent lends its author's access to every colleague who uses it. A user who could not read a table directly can often read it through an agent someone else built, and neither party intended that. Whether the platform supports per-invoker authorisation rather than author-credential execution is the single question worth asking during evaluation.
The authoring surface is also an injection surface: instructions, knowledge sources and connector descriptions are assembled by someone who is not thinking about untrusted input, and a shared agent's knowledge source is frequently a folder anyone can write to. Because no sandbox or runtime enforcement can be inserted into a vendor's execution, every control on the vendor side is a population control — inventory, publication gating, connector policy, and audit that can retire what nobody uses; the runtime controls that survive are the ones on the crossing we run.
distinguishedBy:
Against the API/SDK managed agent runtime: same hosting model, different author. There engineers define agents in code and the delivery pipeline still applies; here the builder UI replaces that pipeline with a publish button, and the unit of concern moves from the definition of one agent to the governance of a population.
Against an internal AI platform you operate: same intent — a paved road for many builders — with the paving done by a vendor. You inherit their guardrails and their environment model, and you cannot add a deployment gate they did not build.

exemplars.name: Microsoft Copilot Studio
exemplars.note: Low-code agent authoring bundled with the productivity suite, available to licensed users by default — verify per tenant which credential mode connectors default to and what the publish gate actually blocks.

exemplars.name: Salesforce Agentforce
exemplars.note: The CRM-embedded builder: agents assembled over platform connectors with the Einstein trust layer as the vendor-side guardrail surface — the zone-2 configuration this page pins.

exemplars.name: Zapier Agents
exemplars.note: The standalone end of the class: a connector marketplace measured in thousands, maker credentials as the natural default, and publication to anyone with the link — the population problem in its purest form.

zones.note: Two populations, and the distinction is the archetype: the colleagues who build agents without being engineers, and the colleagues who then use what they published.
zones.title: User surfaces

zones.note: The platform, and effectively the whole system. Authoring, the orchestrator, the model calls, the sandbox and the connector runtime all execute here — there is no customer-hosted agent runtime on offer. Drawn before our own band because a maker reaches the platform first and the platform reaches back into us second.
zones.title: Vendor platform

zones.note: The narrow strip that is still ours: the gateway a published agent is admitted through, our own tool servers behind it, and the on-premises data gateway for the systems that never leave our network.
zones.title: Enterprise cloud

zones.note: The model the vendor calls on our behalf, and the third-party services their connectors reach.
zones.title: External

zones.note: On a self-service platform this band is population management rather than change review. There is no deployment pipeline to hook into — which is precisely why the platform's own policy engine matters more here than anywhere else in the catalogue.
zones.title: Security & governance control plane

blocks.title: Citizen builder
blocks.note: Someone who is not an engineer, shipping software. No pull request, no pipeline, no review — which is not a gap in their discipline but the product working as designed.

blocks.title: Agent consumers
blocks.note: Colleagues who run what a maker published, usually without knowing who built it or whose access it acts on.

blocks.title: Agent builder platform
blocks.note: One block, because from our side it is one thing: the authoring surface, the orchestrator, the harness, the sandbox and the connector runtime all run in the vendor's cloud. The only part of it we operate is policy configuration, and that is the whole of our leverage.

items.label: Authoring surface
items.note: Where an agent is built and published, by someone who does not think of it as shipping.

items.label: Agent runtime
items.note: Their harness executing the maker's agent, with the model calls theirs to make.

items.label: Connector framework
items.note: Hundreds of prebuilt connectors, executing in their cloud on credentials that are the crux of this page.

blocks.title: AI gateway
blocks.note: Where a published agent is admitted into our systems, and the one hop on that path we run. It carries no inference here — the vendor calls its own model — so this is purely about tools and data, which is the useful distinction from every other gateway in the catalogue.

items.label: MCP & API gateway
items.note: Which of our servers a published agent may reach, and on whose grants.

blocks.title: Tool services
blocks.note: Our own MCP servers and connectors. The platform's MCP path is not a policy bypass — the same data policies that regulate its connectors regulate its MCP tools — but reaching one of ours still needs a publicly resolvable endpoint.

blocks.title: Tunnel connector
blocks.note: The on-premises data gateway — the only on-premises crossing in the architecture, on a host we run beside the gateway and tool services we also run. Outbound-only connections, so nothing is opened inbound. It relays data; it does not run agents, and it has hard payload limits that make it a query path rather than a bulk one. The credentials it caches sit on this host, which is why the secrets pin lands here.

items.label: Outbound connector
items.note: Polls outward; no inbound firewall rule, and a small ceiling on what any one call may carry.

blocks.title: Enterprise data
blocks.note: The systems of record a maker attached as grounding or as an action target — often without anyone asking whether the agent's audience should reach them.

blocks.title: Model provider
blocks.note: The vendor's model, called by the vendor — for the platforms whose model is their own it sits under the same agreement, and this band is external only for the bring-your-own-provider variant. We neither broker it nor hold the key, which is why our own gateway carries no inference on this page. Two variants worth noting in assessment: some platforms run the model entirely inside their own boundary (then this block collapses into the platform and is assured, not drawn), and some let the customer bring a model key — zone-2 configuration that changes whose terms the grounding content leaves under.

blocks.title: Tool services
blocks.note: Third-party services the platform's connectors reach, on whichever credential the maker chose.

blocks.title: Identity services
blocks.note: Whose credentials a published agent runs on, which on this platform is a configuration choice with four answers. End-user credentials are the default and the safe one. Maker credentials are the ambient-authority case: every consumer of that agent transitively inherits the maker's access to the backend. The platform's own inventory records which mode each connector uses, and that field is the single most useful thing an administrator can query here.

blocks.title: Secrets & key management
blocks.note: The tunnel host's cached connection credentials — issued, rotated and revoked from here — and customer-managed keys over the platform's stored data, managed-tier only and slow enough to enable that it is a planned change.

blocks.title: Policy & authorization
blocks.note: The platform's data policies classify every connector and forbid mixing groups across the boundary — and unusually for this catalogue, they have teeth: a violation greys out the publish button outright. Exemptions were removed, so every agent is subject to them.

blocks.title: Supply-chain assurance
blocks.note: The inventory and the publication gate. On a platform where anyone can build, an agent nobody registered is an agent nobody can revoke — and that is the normal case rather than the exception.

blocks.title: Observability & response
blocks.note: Run history, and the population view: which agents exist, who built them, which have outlived their author. The unit of observation here is the population, not a deployment.

edges.label: authors & publishes
edges.note: Built and shipped inside the vendor's surface. No pipeline is involved, so there is no place to insert a review that the platform does not itself provide.

edges.label: uses a published agent
edges.note: Colleagues run what a maker published, on whichever credential the maker configured.

edges.label: their model
edges.note: The vendor calls its own model provider. We are not on this path and hold no key for it, which is why our gateway carries tools and data only.

edges.label: connector calls into our systems
edges.note: The one hop we own. A vendor-hosted agent reaching our data crosses here or it does not reach it at all.

edges.label: brokered tool calls
edges.note: Which of our servers a published agent may call, on grants we scope rather than the maker's standing access.

edges.label: scoped reads & writes
edges.note: Grounding content and action targets, reached on our terms.

edges.label: on-prem query
edges.note: For systems that never leave our network. The gateway relays rather than hosts, and its payload ceiling makes it a query path rather than a bulk one.

edges.label: outbound-only relay
edges.note: Their cloud reaching an on-premises source through software we run. Outbound-only, so nothing is opened inbound.

edges.label: third-party connectors
edges.note: Connectors reaching services outside both environments. This path never touches our network, so the connector policy in their tenant is the only control on it.

risks.note: The defining risk of the archetype, and it materializes in the platform's connection store: a maker attaches a connector on their own credentials and publishes to a team; every consumer then transitively holds the maker's access to that backend. Nobody granted it, nobody sees it in an access review — and most of it plays out on paths our gateway never touches.

An agent is a form away, and the unregistered population accumulates in the platform — not in any one builder. Without the inventory queried, the population is unbounded, and agents outlive the people who built them.
Writes into systems of record from an agent nobody reviewed.

A maker attaches a folder as grounding and the platform indexes it. Whoever can write to that folder can write to the index, and every agent grounded on it reads what they left — the poisoning is of the retrieval source, not of the model.
Grounding content and connector results re-enter the agent as instruction. A document dropped in a shared folder is an instruction channel on this platform.
The on-premises path reaches systems that were never meant to be internet-adjacent, and the credentials it caches sit on a host somebody has to patch.
Grounding content leaves for a model we do not broker and hold no key for.
Publish to a public channel with authentication off and the audience is the internet: the agent's grounding and connectors answer anyone with the URL — found by the thousands by recon tooling.
A document in a grounding folder anyone can write to comes back as a tool result and enters their runtime as instruction — the path the shared-drive scenario walks.
Bulk knowledge upload — folders pushed into the platform as grounding by someone not thinking of it as data movement.

capabilities.note: Whose credentials the agent runs on — end user, maker, on-behalf-of, or a service principal. Default to end-user credentials; maker-provided is the ambient-authority case and should be a deliberate, reviewed exception.

A directory principal minted per published agent, so conditional access, revocation and ownership transfer attach to one agent — the grants live in the platform's connection store, and our gateway sees only the slice it issued.

The cached connection credentials on the tunnel host — issued scoped and short-lived, rotated, and revocable without redeploying the host. Absorbed here per the recorded deviation, because this is where the secret actually sits.
The on-prem query path is scoped like the cloud one: which sources, which rows, whose entitlement — decided before the relay, not assumed from the payload ceiling.
The platform's own inventory, queried rather than assumed — including which connectors use maker credentials, which is the field that finds the ambient-authority agents.

Publication as delivery: versioned agents, a limited audience first, and unpublish as rollback. The data-policy gate that greys out the publish button is admission; this is the release machinery around it.
Runtime confirmation of consequential actions in the consumer's own session, where the platform supports it — the human gate belongs at run time, not at publish time.
Which of our servers a published agent may reach, decided at our tier rather than by the maker.
Classification of what a maker may attach as grounding. The default connector set is the real policy, and a permissive default is a decision nobody remembers making.
Knowing what is behind a connector before it is attachable turns discovery into a decision.
The platform's own grounding and connector-output classification, configured as zone 2 — theirs to implement, ours to switch on and verify, because nothing of ours sits on the connector paths.
Their runtime, their sandbox, their model. Assured by assessment rather than drawn, because none of it is ours to inspect.
Customer-managed keys over the platform's stored data — available on the managed tier only, not retroactive, and slow enough to enable that it is a planned change.
Run history and maker activity, exported where we can query it rather than left in their console.
The population view — every agent somebody built, and which of them still have an owner.
A baseline over run history per agent, because a population of four hundred drifts quietly: the agent whose tool mix changed is the one to quarantine before an incident names it.
Grounding read through our gateway is classified before it goes back to their runtime — the one return leg we can inspect.
Classification before knowledge is attached: a maker uploads whole folders as grounding, and this is the only point where what leaves can still be read.

Invoker-credential execution as the tenant setting: the agent acts on the consumer's grant, never the maker's, wherever the platform supports delegated authorization rather than blanket connector consent.
Disable the app in the tenant and revoke every connector grant — the SaaS form of the stop, and the response the departed-author and shadow-account scenarios actually invoke.
The tenant's configuration drifts as the vendor ships: connector defaults, publication channels and authentication toggles are re-assessed on a clock, not once.

walkthrough.title: An agent is built, published, and used
walkthrough.moves: A colleague assembles an agent from prompts and connectors; another colleague runs it, and the answer comes back.

steps.note: Built and published inside the vendor's surface by someone who is not an engineer. No pipeline is involved, so the platform's own publish gate is the only review there is — and governance here is population management rather than change review.
A colleague runs what was published — on their own credentials if the maker chose end-user auth, and on the maker's if they did not.
Now the model is called — the vendor's own, on its own key, for the running turn. We are not on this path, which is why our gateway carries tools and data only.
The completion comes back into their runtime as the turn's plan.
The one hop we own. A published agent reaching our data crosses here or not at all.
Scoped to grants we decided, rather than to the maker's standing access.
The records the agent was built to reach.
The records come back.
Through our crossing, where the call is recorded.
And out to their runtime as a tool result.
For systems that never leave our network, their cloud reaches an on-premises source through a connector we operate.
A query path rather than a bulk one — the connector caps what any single call carries.
The rows the query asked for, and no more.
Back up the tunnel to their runtime.
The reply returns to the colleague who ran it, grounded on everything the walk touched.

scenarios.title: A maker attaches a connector on their own credentials

steps.note: Prompt written, connectors attached, agent published to a team.
Colleagues run it — and inherit the maker's access to whatever it was attached to. The gap between who built an agent and whose access it uses is where this archetype's incidents live.
Which is only bounded at all because the reach into our systems crosses a tier we run.

scenarios.title: A shared drive becomes an instruction channel

steps.note: A running agent asks for a folder somebody uses as grounding.
Admitted like any other read.
The folder is read.
A document written by anyone with access to that folder comes back with the rest.
It crosses back as an ordinary tool result.
And enters their runtime as model input.
The agent acts on it with the maker's authority — on connectors that never touch our network, so nothing of ours can intervene past this point.

scenarios.title: The author leaves

steps.note: An agent outlives the person who built it, still holding their connector grants.

The maker's third-party grants keep flowing — these never touch our network, so only the platform's connection-ownership transfer or revocation can cut them. That inventory operation is the primary response.
Our gateway cuts the slice it issued — the grants into our own systems — which is real, and is not most of what the departed maker left behind.

scenarios.title: Published to anyone with the link

steps.note: A maker publishes to a public channel and leaves authentication off; the "consumer" is now anyone who finds the URL, and recon tooling finds them by the thousands.
The stranger's question reaches our crossing on the agent's own grants.
Admitted like any run of this agent — the catalogue does not know who is asking.
The grounding answers a stranger. Inventory and publication gating are what would have caught it.

deviations.subject: The vendor band is drawn before our cloud band
deviations.reason: Band order is left-to-right by convention; here the vendor sits first because a maker reaches the platform first and the platform reaches back into us second. The same break, for the same reason, as both SaaS siblings.

deviations.subject: The tunnel absorbs secrets and access scoping
deviations.reason: capabilitySecretsManagement is embodied by the AI gateway, but the on-prem relay never crosses it: the cached connection credentials sit on the tunnel host, so the pin lands there and the issuance story lives in the governance call-out. The tunnel fronts whatever we point it at: the source directly for an on-premises data gateway here, our gateway for MCP-class backends on the enterprise chat drawing — the same component, two chains.

deviations.subject: The AI gateway does not reach a model provider
deviations.reason: Everywhere else in the catalogue the gateway is the model path, and the registered pattern says so. Here it is not: the vendor calls its own model, on its own key, and our gateway exists only to admit a published agent to our tools and data. Drawing an inference leg out of our gateway would assert a broker we do not operate. The model edge is therefore vendor to provider — a property this drawing shares with its two SaaS siblings and the MCP publisher, each recording it the same way. It is drawn with its own items rather than the registered aiGatewayTraffic pack for the same reason: no model proxy, because there is no model traffic to proxy.

deviations.subject: The vendor platform is a single block despite containing an orchestrator, a harness and a sandbox
deviations.reason: The three-zone responsibility rule forbids drawing vendor internals we cannot inspect. On a platform with no customer-hosted runtime option, everything but policy configuration is theirs, so the honest drawing is one block assured by assessment rather than four boxes implying visibility we do not have.

archetypes.title: API/SDK managed agent runtime
summary: A vendor's API-driven hosted agent service: the loop, the memory, the sandbox and the tool gateway supplied as published, separately billed products, driven through an SDK or API rather than a builder UI. The customer owns the front end, the agent definitions, the tools admitted, the identities and the audit export. The governance plane arrives built in, and the trade is that it is configured rather than designed.
description:
Every provider converged on the same decomposition: a runtime, a memory service, a tool gateway, an identity service, a code interpreter and browser, observability, evaluation and policy. That convergence is itself the finding — the governance plane most self-built agent architectures never get is exactly what these services sell. This drawing still shows the provider as one block: the decomposition is documented and separately billed, but under the three-zone rule what they operate inside their boundary is assured rather than drawn, and their tool gateway, memory and sandbox appear as the block's items — zone-2 surfaces we configure, not tiers we run. The loop's execution behind them remains genuinely uninspectable.
The consequential choice is between the managed harness and the code escape hatch. Every provider offers both: a declarative agent whose loop they run, and a bring-your-own-code runtime where they supply the sandbox and the identity but the loop is the customer's. The first inherits the platform's guardrails automatically; the second inherits only what it explicitly calls. Teams routinely start with the first, hit a limitation, move to the second, and do not notice which controls stopped applying.
Managed memory is the component most likely to be switched on without a decision. Its scope — per session, per user, or shared across users — is a configuration flag with a data-protection consequence, and cross-user scope means one user's content can shape another's turn.
The baseline this page targets is a distinct agent identity: a first-class, revocable principal per agent, separate from the service and from the user, carrying on-behalf-of user context per session. Platforms that supply that as a service make it the genuine advantage of buying the runtime; platforms whose only identity is a credential vault entry are a deficient variant — the agent then "is" whatever the vault holds, and the deficiency is a named finding in the exemplar assessment, not a second architecture. The costs either way are portability and opacity: the policy language moves to no other provider, and debugging a misbehaviour means reading traces rather than code.
distinguishedBy:
Against building the agent tier: the same components with the provider supplying them. The work moves from designing an identity model, a policy engine and a sandbox to configuring three, and from having to build observability to having to export it.
Against the UI/low-code managed agent runtime: same hosting model, different author. Here engineers define agents in code against an SDK or API, and the software-delivery pipeline — review, versioning, staged rollout — still applies to the definition even though the loop is the vendor's. The low-code sibling replaces that pipeline with a builder UI and a publish button, which moves the risk from the definition to the population.

exemplars.name: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
exemplars.note: The hyperscaler decomposition in full — runtime, memory, gateway, identity, browser and code interpreter as separately billed services, with Cedar default-deny policy enforced at the provider's tool gateway. Verify identity, retention, vault-scoping and customer-key behaviour per component before relying on any of them.

exemplars.name: Vertex AI Agent Engine
exemplars.note: A managed runtime with admin-enforced guardrail floors (Model Armor) — the zone-2 configuration surface this page pins, shipped as platform policy.

zones.note: The people the published agent serves, and the team that defined it.
zones.title: User surfaces

zones.note: The provider's environment, and where the agent actually runs. Drawn before our own band because that is the direction of the work: a request reaches the vendor first, and the vendor reaches back into us second. What they operate inside it is assured, not drawn.
zones.title: Vendor platform

zones.note: What we still own on somebody else's platform: the definition that decides what the agent may do, the gateway that admits it back into our systems, and the systems themselves.
zones.title: Enterprise cloud

zones.note: Where the agent's actions land outside both environments.
zones.title: External

zones.note: On a platform we do not operate, this band is most of what "our controls" can mean — and the identity the agent runs as is not one of them by default.
zones.title: Security & governance control plane

blocks.title: Developer
blocks.note: The engineer who writes the definition and the code — the author the delivery pipeline still applies to, which is this page's whole distinction from the low-code sibling.

blocks.title: End user
blocks.note: The person a session runs for, and whose credentials it acts on if we set it up that way.

blocks.title: Application front end
blocks.note: The customer-owned surface an SDK-driven runtime is invoked from — our code, calling their API. User authentication and the delegated session context are bound here, before anything reaches the vendor.

items.label: App & API endpoint
items.note: The published surface our users actually touch.

items.label: Identity binding
items.note: Which of our people a session runs for, established before it starts.

blocks.title: Managed runtime
blocks.note: The provider hosts the agent loop itself — tool-call decisions, error recovery, context compaction — along with session state and a sandbox per session. Defined declaratively over an API rather than shipped as a container, which makes the definition the whole of the behaviour contract. The adoption caveats are product-specific and belong in the exemplar assessment rather than here — retention and compliance eligibility of cloud sessions, vault scoping, and key-management exclusions all vary by provider and change by quarter; verify each per product before relying on it.

items.label: Agent loop
items.note: Their harness running our definition, with the reasoning and the retries theirs to operate.

items.label: Memory store
items.note: Session and long-term state they hold, whose scope is a configuration flag rather than an architecture.

items.label: Sandboxed tools
items.note: Provider-operated code execution and browsing, one container per session — with its own path to the open web that never touches anything we run.

items.label: Remote MCP & connectors
items.note: Their tool gateway: hosted MCP servers and connectors the provider calls from its own side, the tool list fetched by them. That path never touches our network — only the tools we choose to front cross our gateway — so the risk sits on this item and the control is the default-deny policy their gateway lets us set.

blocks.title: Agent definition & code
blocks.note: Model, prompt, tools, MCP servers and skills, declared and pushed to the provider. On a runtime we do not operate this artifact is very nearly the whole of what we control about the agent, which makes reviewing it a release gate rather than a formality.

items.label: Declarative definition
items.note: What the agent may do, in a form somebody can read and approve before it ships.

items.label: Custom loop code
items.note: The escape hatch: a bring-your-own-code runtime inherits only the guardrails it explicitly calls — same deploy edge, thinner enforcement, per the bypass scenario.

blocks.title: AI gateway
blocks.note: The customer-operated crossing where a vendor-hosted agent is admitted into our systems. The one component on that path we run, and therefore the only place the reach is scoped, credentialed and recorded on our terms rather than theirs.

items.label: MCP & API gateway
items.note: Which of our servers a hosted agent may reach, and on whose grants.

blocks.title: Tool services
blocks.note: Our own MCP servers and connectors — the repositories, ticketing and systems of record a hosted agent is adopted in order to reach.

blocks.title: Enterprise data
blocks.note: The systems of record behind those servers, reached on grants we scope per session.

blocks.title: Tool services
blocks.note: Third-party servers and connectors our gateway brokers outward — the same component as the internal surface, out where nobody we contracted with operates it.

blocks.title: Downstream services
blocks.note: Where an action lands outside both environments, and where untrusted content returns from.

blocks.title: Identity services
blocks.note: The baseline: a first-class, revocable principal per agent with on-behalf-of user context, supplied by the platform. Where a product's only identity is a vault entry, that is a deficiency the assessment names — and mapping its credentials back to our own records becomes ours to maintain.

blocks.title: Secrets & key management
blocks.note: Per-user credential vaults and customer-managed keys over the platform's data — with the product-specific caveats (vault scoping, key exclusions) verified per exemplar rather than assumed of the class.

blocks.title: Policy & authorization
blocks.note: What the hosted agent may reach in our systems, decided at our gateway rather than in their console — and the per-tool approval their connector configuration defaults to, which is worth leaving on.

blocks.title: Supply-chain assurance
blocks.note: Definition admission, the behavioural checks in front of every change, staged rollout of the definitions themselves, and the platform assessment behind adopting the runtime at all — the change half of governance, kept apart from the traces.

blocks.title: Observability & response
blocks.note: Their session event log fused with our gateway's record. A trail that exists only in their console is one we cannot query during an incident.

edges.label: authored & reviewed
edges.note: The definition arrives through the ordinary delivery pipeline — written, reviewed, versioned — which is the property this whole page's distinction rests on.

edges.label: request / response
edges.note: Our users touch our surface: the front end binds who a session runs for before anything reaches the vendor, and the response returns the same way.

edges.label: session invoke
edges.note: Our code invokes their runtime over the SDK, carrying the delegated user context the front end bound. The vendor-direct variant — no customer tier at all — is real for one exemplar class and recorded as a deviation, not drawn as a second path.

edges.label: deploy
edges.note: One direction: the definition is pushed into an environment we do not operate. What it declares is the behaviour contract, and reviewing it is the last point at which we decide anything about the agent itself.

edges.label: back into our systems
edges.note: The crossing this architecture exists to govern. Their runtime reaches our gateway rather than reaching past it, so the grants are ours to scope and ours to revoke. The direct invoke form is drawn; the tunnel form — an outbound-only connector we run inside our network — is the enterprise chat drawing's Tunnel connector, by reference.

edges.label: brokered tool calls
edges.note: Which of our servers a hosted agent may call, on short-lived grants we issue.

edges.label: scoped reads & writes
edges.note: The repositories and records the agent was adopted to work on.

edges.label: brokered external calls
edges.note: Third-party servers and connectors, reached through the crossing that admitted them — egress and returned-content classification enforced at our boundary.

edges.label: action / returned content
edges.note: Actions landing outside, and the content they return.

edges.label: sandbox browsing
edges.note: The provider's hosted browser and code interpreter reach the open web from their environment — a path that never touches anything we run, and this archetype's dominant untrusted ingress.

risks.note: Their infrastructure exercising our authority. The grant is the only thing bounding it, and the grant is issued at our gateway — which is the entire argument for drawing one.

Requests, context and tool results all live on their side, under their retention terms — and managed memory's scope is a configuration flag: cross-user scope means one user's content shapes another's turn, switched on without anyone deciding it.

Where the product falls short of the identity baseline — a vault entry instead of a principal — a credential that outlives the person it belonged to keeps acting as them, and nothing in the platform ties it to a lifecycle.
An agent is an API call away. Without a registry the population is unbounded and invisible, and the definition is the only artifact that ever existed for review.
Writes into systems of record from a loop running somewhere we cannot watch.
Content returning from a brokered outbound action re-enters a context we do not hold.
The hosted browser reads the open web straight into the loop, vendor-side — the dominant untrusted ingress of this archetype, on a path with no customer control anywhere.
Tool descriptions fetched vendor-side enter the loop as instruction, from servers named in the definition and vetted by nobody on the path.
The delegation boundary: a service credential substituted for the user's context here means every downstream grant is the service's, not the person's.
A record somebody else authored comes back as a tool result and enters their runtime as instruction — classified at our gateway on the way, which is the only reason it can be.

capabilities.note: Which of our people a session runs for, established at our front end before it starts.

A first-class, revocable principal per agent with on-behalf-of context — the platform capability worth selecting for; where it is missing, the vault entry is the identity and needs the lifecycle the platform will not give it.
Per-user vaults rather than a service credential, and the placeholder-substituted kind where the platform offers it, so the secret is swapped in at egress and the agent never holds the value.
Customer-managed keys over their storage — with the exclusion recorded: vault credential values sit under their keys, not ours.
Every definition registered and reviewed before deploy; there is no other artifact to review. Change-gating on the data path, per the recorded deviation.
Immutable versions, a canary alias, and rollback that is a pointer flip — the software-delivery half of this page's distinction, applied to the definition.
Which servers, which tools, whose grant — decided at our tier because theirs is not ours to configure.

Our gateway owns the gate: a consequential write is refused unless it carries an approval bound to the exact action — surfaced to the approver through our front end, with the vendor's per-tool approval defaults as the second, configured layer.
The gateway's registry of external destinations for the tools we chose to front — the subset that crosses our gateway. Hosted tools the provider calls from its own side never meet this list.
Returned tool and connector content is classified at our crossing before it goes back to a loop we cannot see — enterprise-data returns included, because many hands wrote those records too.
Their isolation, retention and tenancy assured by assessment rather than drawn — the only representation a vendor-internal control gets.
Their session event log exported and fused with our own record, so an incident has one queryable trail — assembled here, off the data path.
Retained on our side, because a trail only in their console is one we cannot search.
Their runtime applies the model-side checks; ours is a zone-2 configuration choice on their surface rather than a tier we operate.
Memory scope is a flag on their platform, and the default is wider than most adopters assume. Setting it deliberately is the whole control.
Behavioural checks against the definition before it ships, since the definition is all we control.
The population view across every agent somebody deployed with an API call.
Default-deny policy at their tool gateway — the floor a builder cannot lower, set in the tenant rather than enforced by us.
Per-session and per-user ceilings before the vendor meters the loop — a hosted browser steered into an open-ended run bills by the minute.
Disable the app in the tenant and revoke every connector grant — the SaaS form of the stop, and the response the departed-author and shadow-account scenarios actually invoke.
The platform's defaults drift as it ships — memory scope, guardrail coverage, tool-gateway policy — and are re-assessed on a clock, not once.

walkthrough.title: A user's request becomes a tool call on our systems
walkthrough.moves: A request through our front end to a runtime somebody else operates, reaching back into our data, and the answer coming home.

steps.note: The request arrives at our surface, and the session is bound to one of our people.
Our code invokes their runtime, carrying the delegated user context.
Their runtime reaches our gateway rather than reaching past it into the tool surface.
Admitted to a named server on a short-lived, per-user grant.
The read or write happens on our side, which is the only reason it is bounded.
The record comes back.
Through the crossing, where the call is recorded against the per-user grant.
Outbound actions leave through the same crossing, against the named-destination list.
The effect lands outside.
What returns starts its way back.
And is classified at our gateway before the hosted loop reads it as instruction.
The tool results land in their runtime, which finishes the turn.
The completion returns to our front end.
And to the person the session ran for, attributable end to end.

scenarios.title: A credential outlives its owner

steps.note: An agent is deployed on a platform whose identity is a vault reference, not a principal.
Sessions keep presenting that credential after the person has gone, because nothing in the platform ties it to their lifecycle.
Our gateway is where that can be noticed and cut, since it is the only hop we watch.

scenarios.title: The hosted browser reads the web

steps.note: The sandbox browses on the vendor's side — no customer control sits anywhere on the path.
Untrusted content enters the loop as instruction.
A steered loop now asks our gateway for tools — the first tier we control, and the reason its per-call policy cannot assume a well-behaved caller.
Scope, approval and the record are what stand between the steered plan and our data.

scenarios.title: The definition moves to custom code

steps.note: The team hits a limitation and ships the escape hatch: their sandbox, their identity, but the loop is now our code — and it inherits only the guardrails it explicitly calls.
Calls still arrive here, which is why our per-call policy is the floor that survives the migration — the platform's automatic guardrails did not.

deviations.subject: The vendor band is drawn before our cloud band
deviations.reason: Band order is left-to-right by convention; here the vendor sits first because that is the direction of the work — a session reaches the vendor's runtime and the vendor reaches back into us second. The same break, for the same reason, as the low-code sibling.

deviations.subject: Definition admission, evaluation and staged rollout are pinned on the deploy edge
deviations.reason: All three are management-class capabilities cited from the supply-chain call-out, but what they gate — the definition — genuinely flows through the deploy edge, the ontology's own change-gating exception. The chips sit where the gate closes.

deviations.subject: One exemplar class is vendor-direct and has no customer front end
deviations.reason: Hosted background coding agents take a task and a grant and are driven from the vendor's own surfaces; for that class the endUser reaches the provider directly and the front-end tier this drawing requires does not exist. Recorded rather than drawn as a second topology — its compensating posture is the narrow repository grant.

deviations.subject: The AI gateway carries tool and data traffic only
deviations.reason: The provider calls its own model inside its own runtime — no Model provider block exists on this drawing — and nothing fetches skills through our crossing. The gateway is drawn with its one real traffic class rather than the registered aiGatewayTraffic pack, following the low-code builder's precedent: the honest signal that a gateway is not on the model path is its own contents.

deviations.subject: Hosted tools are an item on the runtime, not an edge to the external band
deviations.reason: Hosted MCP servers and connectors are called from the provider's side and never touch our network — the low-code sibling draws that as a platform-to-tools edge. Here the runtime's external reach is drawn once already (the hosted browser), and a second vendor-side arrow would cross the front end. The item carries the provenance risk and the zone-2 policy control; nothing of ours sits on the path either way.

guidance.attribution: Authored in this repository. Pattern-level by design; no vendor facts to date.
overview: This is the architecture where the agent writes: a request arrives, a decision happens, and an effect lands on a system of record in seconds with nobody between them. The organisation's requirements therefore centre on reversibility rather than accuracy — the review question for every design is not "how often is it right" but "what happens when it is wrong, and who can undo it, and how fast."

The requirements below assume the multi-agent workflow's guidance as a sibling: each subagent there is this pattern one level down, and everything here applies inside every one of them. What this pattern adds is the concentrated question of a single fast path — the action catalogue, the approval threshold and the compensating transaction carry the weight a human carries in the chat pattern and durability machinery carries in the workflow pattern.

items.title: Make the action catalogue the policy surface — no arbitrary calls
body: Require a deterministic catalogue: named, parameter-validated actions, each declaring its blast radius and its compensating transaction. An agent that can compose arbitrary API calls has no policy surface at all — reject that design in review, whatever the framework makes convenient. Enforcement is per invocation, outside the loop: this action, this record, this value, now — evaluated by a policy engine the agent cannot edit, not a session-time grant. Evidence: the catalogue definition, and a denied-call log showing the bounds actually fire.

items.title: Tie approval to consequence, and reversal to everything else
body: The approval threshold is keyed to irreversibility and value, never to model confidence — and it must be rare enough that a human actually reads what fires. Below the threshold, the control is the compensating transaction: an action with no reversal path does not belong in the catalogue below the gate. Assessment probe: list the catalogue's actions and demand the compensating transaction for each; any blank cell below the threshold fails the review.

items.title: Give the agent an identity, and broker every credential
body: A distinct, revocable workload identity per agent — actions taken as a shared service account are neither attributable nor separately revocable, and turn every incident response into a full-service outage. The agent tier holds no standing keys: model and tool credentials are brokered at the gateway per call, short-lived and scoped. Effective authority on any call is the intersection of the grant the trigger carried, the agent's identity, the action policy and the target record — never the union. Assessment probe: revoke the agent's identity and confirm the loop stops without touching any other service.

items.title: Scope what the loop reads, because the payload's author is the attacker
body: The payload that starts a run is authored by the party who benefits from the outcome, and record content written months earlier re-enters as context — both are injection paths with a short path to money. Classify inbound payloads before the loop, scope retrieval to the account under discussion rather than to what the service can reach, and keep case memory hard-scoped to one case. Assessment probe: a request against account A that attempts to retrieve account B's records into context.

items.title: Bind identity at the trigger ingress, and admit actions out of band
body: Whose authority a run carries is established at ingress, before the loop runs — a service principal with its own named scope, or the on-behalf-of grant attached to the message. It is the identity every downstream action is taken on behalf of, and the thing that bounds the reachable set. There is no front end to bind it anywhere else. The catalogue itself changes only out of band: actions exist because the registry admitted them, through a review the loop cannot invoke — admission, not discovery. Assessment probe: have the model name a plausible action that was never admitted, and confirm the gateway refuses it.

items.title: Evaluate every change, the prompt included
body: With nobody watching a run, there is no later opportunity to notice a change was wrong: every model, prompt or catalogue change ships through a behavioural evaluation gate first. The system instruction is versioned and owned like the catalogue it governs — a prompt edit is a behaviour change and gets the same review.

items.title: Bound the spend, the destinations, and the time to stop
body: Rate and budget ceilings sit at the gateway, sized for a loop that retries in seconds; the write path reaches named destinations only, because unbounded egress is the exfiltration channel a steered agent looks for. The decision audit records action, reasoning, inputs and identity where the agent can append and cannot amend — the basis for reversal and dispute. And the stop must halt the agent and revoke its identity without a deploy, because the loop acts faster than a pipeline ships.

guidance.attribution: Authored in this repository. Protocol claims follow A2A v1.0 (March 2026) and the OAuth token-exchange and identity-assertion drafts it leaves the identity work to; adoption claims are stated as the early state they are.
overview: A2A defines discovery (a signed Agent Card), work (tasks, messages, artifacts) and which authentication schemes a peer accepts, and deliberately stops there: credentials are obtained out of band, the authenticated identity is the calling agent rather than its user, card signing is optional, and per-skill authorization is left to whatever sits in front of the agent. Every requirement below is that missing identity layer, made mandatory by our policy rather than by the protocol.

Two identities travel on every task and are never confused: the agent's (a registered client with a private key or a mutual-TLS certificate, one per relationship) and the user's (an identity assertion the peer's platform can verify because it federates with our identity provider — or nothing, and the person is asked). Authority never propagates: every hop gets a token bound to that hop's audience and skill, exchanged at our authorization server and logged as a delegation step.

items.title: Give every agent an identity of its own, per relationship
body: Require our harness to be registered as a client in each peer platform under its own identity, authenticating with `private_key_jwt` or mutual TLS — never a shared secret, never a human's session — with the key held by the secrets service and rotated. Require the same of every peer agent we admit: a registered client with a key, scopes limited to the skills it was admitted for, an owner and a decommission date. Inside a trust boundary, mutual TLS; across one, OAuth 2.0 with sender-constrained tokens where the peer supports them, so a bearer lifted from a log cannot be replayed. Evidence: the registration record on each side, a token from a test task showing agent identity, audience and skill scope, and the key rotation log.

items.title: Let the user's identity travel only where it is honoured, and never further
body: Decide federation per peer platform in the identity provider's registry: which peers may be told about which users. Where federation exists, the user's login is exchanged at our authorization server for an assertion whose audience is the peer's authorization server, whose subject is the user and whose scope is the one skill being invoked — the JWT-bearer grant at the peer's token endpoint, no browser, no per-peer consent. Where it does not, the user's identity does not travel: the task stops in `TASK_STATE_AUTH_REQUIRED` and the person authenticates to the peer themselves, in their own session, and our agent never holds that credential. Inbound, the same discipline: a peer's token is exchanged for a downstream token naming our tool server, the skill and the peer's tenant before our systems are touched. Assessment probe: send a task to a federated peer and confirm the token the peer received names our user and one skill; send one to an unfederated peer and confirm the person, not our agent, was asked.

items.title: Admit cards; never discover them live
body: A peer's Agent Card is admitted into the gateway's registry by an owner: JWS signature verified against a published key, hash pinned, skills, `securitySchemes`, token endpoint and bindings reviewed, and the assessment behind the platform agreement on file. Every task begins by re-verifying the card; a changed hash stops the task and alerts the owner, because a moved token endpoint is how a redirected card steals every credential sent to it. Publish our own card signed, with the key discoverable, and treat a change to it as a release. Assessment probe: alter a pinned card's token endpoint in a test registry and confirm the next task is refused and the owner notified.

items.title: Enforce per-skill authorization at the crossing, in both directions
body: The protocol says scopes SHOULD grant access to some skills and not others and leaves enforcement to us. Require the gateway to enforce it: which peer may invoke which of our skills, which of a peer's skills our agent may invoke for which users, decided per task against the token's scope. Meter per peer, per task and per skill, because a peer's agent that retries or fans out is another organisation's loop spending our budget. Inspect the outbound task payload and the inbound artifacts as the boundary crossings they are. Assessment probe: a valid peer token for skill A invoking skill B, and a task payload carrying a record the user may not export.

items.title: Treat everything a peer returns as content, and store nothing unclassified
body: Artifacts, status messages and card descriptions are text composed by a model another organisation runs; they land in our agent's context as instruction. Classify at the crossing with the peer's identity attached, write to memory only after classification and scoped to the task, and keep consequential actions behind the person regardless of how many agents recommended them. Assessment probe: an artifact containing an instruction to call a third agent, and confirmation that the loop surfaced it rather than acted on it.

items.title: Make one audit trail out of two organisations' logs, and be able to cut a peer off
body: Carry W3C trace context and the task id on every hop and require the peer to do the same as part of the agreement, so a delegation chain that spans two audits can be read as one — the delegation-chain opacity OWASP names is otherwise exactly this. Log every task in and out with peer, user, skill, scope and outcome. Revocation is one action at the registry and the authorization server, made real for issued tokens by introspection and short lifetimes. Assessment probe: revoke a test peer and confirm its next call fails within one token lifetime and its card is no longer served as a peer's.

guidance.attribution: Authored in this repository. Pattern-level by design; no vendor facts to date.
overview: This is the pattern most organisations mean by "hosting agents": a durable orchestration loop with subagents, calling tools across business data connectors, running on infrastructure you operate. Because it is built rather than bought, the organisation's controls are architectural requirements — properties the design must have before it ships, enforced in review and in the platform the workload runs on.

The neighbouring archetype matters for scoping: the single agent workflow — one agent on one fast path, reading a request, deciding and writing to systems of record in seconds, with no supervisor, journal or replay — is not a contrast to this pattern but a nesting: each subagent here is that diagram one level down. The requirements below are the durability-and-supervision layer this pattern adds; the single-agent pattern's own controls (the action catalogue, reversibility thresholds, compensating transactions) still apply inside every subagent and get their own guidance.

items.title: Route every tool call through one governed gateway
body: Require a single choke point between agents and tools: one gateway that owns the tool catalogue, scopes each agent to the least set of tools its job needs, and is the only path — a subagent with its own side-channel to a connector is the design smell to reject in review. The registry behind the gateway is the inventory of record: which agents exist, which tools each may call, and who approved the pairing.

items.title: Give agents their own identity and short-lived credentials
body: Each agent and subagent acts as a non-human identity of its own — never a shared service account, and never a borrowed human session. Connector access is granted to that identity, scoped and revocable in the directory; credentials are issued ephemerally at call time from a secrets service rather than living in the agent's environment or prompt. Define effective authority as an intersection: the agent's own identity, the on-behalf-of grant the triggering request carried when a human's authority started the run, the workflow's policy, and the current step's scope — never the union of any of them. Runs started by events alone carry an explicit service principal with its own named scope, not a leftover human grant. The test worth applying in review: when this agent is compromised, what standing access does the attacker hold? The right answer is close to none.

items.title: Authorize actions at runtime, keep humans on the escalation path, and meter it
body: The model's plan is a proposal; a policy layer outside the model decides. Require runtime authorization on tool calls (policy on the action, its arguments and its target, not just on tool identity), human approval on the classes of action the organisation names as irreversible or sensitive, and rate, quota and spend limits per agent — an agent loop that can retry is a denial-of-wallet incident waiting for a bug.

items.title: Treat retrieved content as input, and inspect what leaves
body: Everything the connectors return — documents, records, messages — enters the context window as unauthenticated content that can steer the loop. Require injection screening on retrieved content and on inter-agent messages, and data-loss inspection on what flows out through responses and tool calls, at the gateway where both directions already pass.

items.title: Scope durable state, and keep secrets out of the journal
body: The journal persists everything a step returns, and shared memory is cross-step instruction. Require run-scoped memory that later steps read as untrusted input; ban secrets from step returns, because the journal cannot un-learn them; and fence every side effect with an idempotency key, because replay is a feature of the engine — a payment step that is not fenced executes twice on recovery, correctly, by design.

items.title: Evaluate change before it runs unattended, and read the traces while it runs
body: A model, prompt or agent change ships through a behavioural evaluation gate, because a process that runs for days offers no later moment to notice the change was wrong. The delegation graph must be legible after the fact — which agent decided what, on whose behalf, what it handed to the next one — assembled from gateway and engine traces. And somebody, or something, correlates those traces while the process is still running: coordinated fan-out, anomalous delegation and autonomous persistence are visible in the record only if it is actually read.

items.title: Bound where output can land, and where generated code runs
body: Outbound calls reach named destinations only — over a process that runs for days, unbounded egress gives a steered agent all the time it needs to find the exit. Agents write code; only the sandbox runs it: an isolated runtime with its own filesystem and network, admitted through the registry like any tool, torn down per task so nothing accumulates between runs.

items.title: Log for reconstruction, and build the stop before you need it
body: The audit requirement is reconstruction: from any effect on a business system, walk back through the tool call, the agent, the triggering context and the originating request. Structured, tamper-resistant logs at the gateway make that a query rather than an investigation. Pair it with a stop path that is designed, not improvised — quarantine one agent, revoke its identity and credentials, drain or halt its queued work — and exercise it before the first incident does.

guidance.attribution: Authored in this repository. Pattern-level by design; no vendor facts to date.
overview: A chat agent's security posture rests on one fact: the human reads every reply before the next action. Every requirement below either protects that gate (proposals worth reading, prompts rare enough to read), respects the delegated authority model (the tools act as the conversing user, never as the service), or bounds the conversation itself — which is a persistence surface where one poisoned tool result steers every later turn.

The bright line to police in review: remove the human from the turns — a scheduled run, an auto-approve setting, a background continuation — and the deployment has silently become the single agent workflow and must meet that pattern's requirements instead. The most common governance failure in this archetype is not a missing control; it is a chat agent that stopped being one without anybody re-reviewing it.

items.title: Keep the in-thread approval worth reading
body: The approval is only a control if the proposal is specific — "OK to proceed?" approves nothing in particular. Require action proposals that name the operation, the target and the consequence, and keep them rare: a gate that fires on every step trains the user to accept, which is this architecture's version of no gate at all. Assessment probe: read a week of approval prompts and count how many a reviewer could distinguish.

items.title: Every tool call carries the user's grant, not the service's reach
body: Authority is on-behalf-of: a delegated grant scoped to the session and the user, evaluated per call, ending when the session ends. The agent tier keeps its own workload identity — distinct from the users it serves — and holds no standing keys; the gateway brokers user-scoped credentials per call. Assessment probe: a user who cannot read a record directly asks the agent for it; the tool call must fail with the user's entitlement, not succeed with the service's.

items.title: Treat the conversation as a persistence surface
body: Context accumulates — retrievals, tool results, uploads — and all of it stands beside the system instruction on every later call. Scope memory to the conversation and the user with no cross-session reads; classify returned content before it re-enters the thread; and redact what a session may accumulate, because a late question can surface records the current topic never needed. Assessment probe: plant an instruction in a record the agent will retrieve, and verify classification catches it before the next model call.

items.title: Render output as content, and bound where it can go
body: The thread renders model output in a browser: sanitise markup and links before display, because a rendered image URL exfiltrates the conversation without a click. On the action side, tools reach named destinations only — the documented exfiltration chains in this archetype end at an attacker's collection endpoint that an egress allowlist would have refused.

items.title: Admit tools out of band, and evaluate change before the thread meets it
body: Tools exist in a conversation because the registry admitted them, through a review the conversation cannot invoke. Every model, prompt or tool change ships through a behavioural evaluation gate first, because the thing being changed decides the next action a human is asked to approve.

items.title: Ground the thread on an index somebody defends
body: Retrieval runs with the asking user's permissions, never the service's — the index must not become a way to read what the conversation's owner cannot. Guard what enters the corpus as much as what leaves it: content planted in an indexed source returns as trusted grounding. And because replies drive approvals, check the reply's claims against the sources it cites — verifying what the human is told, distinct from what the agent may do.

items.title: Meter the edge, audit off the thread, and be able to stop
body: Session and per-user ceilings sit at the entry point, because per-token inference behind a public chat surface is a spend problem before it is anything else. The audit trail — proposal, approval, action — is recorded off the agent's write path; the thread the user sees is not the audit record. The stop ends live sessions and revokes the agent's identity without a deploy.

guidance.attribution: Authored in this repository. Protocol claims follow the 2026-07-28 MCP revision, its authorization security considerations, and the stable enterprise-managed authorization extension (ID-JAG, June 2026); pattern-level by design.
overview: A published MCP server is an OAuth resource server whose clients are language models: conventional multi-tenant service engineering, plus a small set of inversions that follow from the caller being a model. The tool descriptions you publish execute as instruction inside somebody else's agent; the arguments you receive were composed by a model that may have been steered; and the user who consented is not present at call time. Every requirement below is either ordinary service discipline applied with unusual force, or a direct consequence of one of those three facts.

The deployment shape to require is boring on purpose: a gateway tier in front, identity federated to the enterprise IdP, one stateless application, a secrets manager behind it, and a governance plane that owns scopes, tool text, registry listing, audit and revocation. Teams should not be designing novel session schemes or token flows — the protocol deleted sessions and specifies the auth model; the review question is whether the build matches it.

items.title: Front the endpoint, and decide the three identity flows before any tool code is written
body: Require a gateway tier in front of the service: WAF, per-client and per-tenant rate limits sized for machine callers, and routing on the protocol's method and tool-name headers so metering never needs to parse bodies. Then require the build to name which of the three caller types it serves and implement each by the book. Enterprise callers: enterprise-managed authorization — single sign-on at the IdP, an ID-JAG exchanged there under the administrator's app registry and policy, redeemed at our authorization server with the JWT-bearer grant, no per-server consent. Public clients with no prior relationship: the authorization-code grant with PKCE (S256), `resource` on both requests, a client-ID metadata document as the client identity, `iss` checked on the response, and a consent screen that names the client and its redirect host. Autonomous workloads: `client_credentials` with `private_key_jwt` under the workload's own registered identity, with scopes narrower than any user's. Dynamic client registration is deprecated and fails review. Evidence: the gateway config, the IdP's app-registry entry for this server, the authorization-server metadata showing the grant profiles, and one token per flow from a test client showing audience, expiry and scopes.

Tokens are validated on every request — signature or introspection, audience equals this server's canonical URI, expiry, scope against the tool being called, subject — and audience validation is the server's own obligation even when the gateway pre-checks. Prefer introspection where revocation must reach running agents; local JWT validation is faster and blind to it. A server that accepts a token issued for any other audience fails the assessment.

Scopes are a catalogue owned outside the service: narrow, no omnibus scope, minimal set at first grant, and every scope an operation needs emitted in one `insufficient_scope` challenge so the client steps up in one round trip. Under enterprise-managed authorization a step-up is another exchange at the IdP, and the organisation's policy answers; under the public flow it is a consent screen listing exactly the added scope. Assessment probe: call a write tool with a read token and confirm a single 403 challenge names every scope the write needs.

items.title: Build stateless; a state handle is a name, not a capability
body: The current protocol has no sessions: every request is self-contained, which is what makes the tier horizontally scalable. Where tools need cross-call state, the server mints opaque handles — high-entropy, bound to the token's subject, expiring, and re-authorized against the presenting token on every request. Possession of a handle must prove nothing. Reject designs that carry trust in the handle, vary tool listings per connection, or reimplement session affinity. Require Origin validation and TLS termination evidence at the edge. Assessment probe: present a valid handle with a different subject's token and confirm the request fails.

items.title: The caller's token never travels upstream
body: Most servers wrap existing systems, and the one rule with no exceptions is at that boundary: the inbound token stops at the service. Two shapes pass review. On-behalf-of: the handler exchanges the inbound token at the authorization server for one whose audience is the upstream and whose scope is narrowed to the tool, so the upstream sees who is really asking and applies its own authorization — the preferred shape for internal systems that already understand the user. Service credential: the handler calls as itself on a credential the secrets manager issues, scopes and rotates, where no delegation exists. The third shape — forwarding the inbound token — is the confused deputy the protocol forbids by name, and the finding most often discovered in production. Bound egress to named upstream destinations; unbounded outbound reach from a tool server is the exfiltration path a steered agent is looking for.

On the data path, require the dual check on every operation — the scope permits it, and the tenant on the token matches the tenant on the record — enforced in a shared layer rather than re-implemented per handler. Assessment probe: a valid token for tenant A requesting tenant B's record by identifier, on a read as well as a write.

items.title: Ship tool text like code, and list the server like a dependency
body: Descriptions, schemas and error text execute inside the caller's model, so they ship through the same pipeline as code: versioned, reviewed as a security artifact, adversarially read for what a model will do with the words, and published with provenance. Publish to the registry or private subregistry consuming clients admit from, with versions pinned, so a definition that changes after approval is detectable by the people trusting it. Make consequential handlers return `input_required` and execute only on the retry that carries the confirmation — annotations are hints a client must treat as untrusted, so elicitation is the lever the server actually holds — and keep results bounded in size, because output lands in someone else's context window.

items.title: Test it like the published application it is
body: Behind the protocol this is an ordinary HTTP application with ordinary attack surface, and it ships through the ordinary release gate: dependency and code scanning, dynamic testing against the deployed endpoint, and the tenant-isolation checks exercised as tests rather than trusted as intentions. A tool server that skipped AppSec because "it is just MCP" skipped it for the one application whose caller is a machine that retries.

items.title: Audit per call, and design revocation before launch
body: The audit record is per tool call — client, user, tenant, tool, arguments, result, with trace context propagated — because it is both the incident trail and the answer to a customer asking what their agent did. Scope design is where a hijacked agent's blast radius is decided: a catalogue of narrow scopes owned outside the service, no omnibus scope, and step-up challenges rather than over-asking at consent. Revocation must work at three grains without a deploy: a user (at the IdP — a group removal ends every new ID-JAG at once), a client (at the authorization server), and a tool (at the definition layer) — and it must reach tokens already issued, which is what introspection, short access-token lifetimes and rotating refresh tokens buy. Assessment probe: remove a test user from the granting group and confirm the agent's next call fails within one token lifetime, and that its refresh and re-exchange both fail.

guidance.attribution: Authored in this repository. Pattern-level by design; serving products are named only in cited sources, not in the items.
overview: Self-hosting open weights trades a data-disclosure risk for a supply-chain, availability and safety risk: no provider applies content policy, absorbs spikes, or patches the serving stack. The requirements below are the provider role, written down — and the two facts that shape them are that the serving stacks assume a trusted network (auth is partial, auxiliary endpoints and distributed control planes ship open by design), and that multi-tenancy inside the runtime is a set of configuration flags with data-protection consequences.

The review posture: treat serving configuration as security configuration. Continuous batching, cache sharing, tenancy scoping and network binding are tuning knobs to the platform team and controls to the security team; the gap between those two readings is where the incidents in this archetype live.

items.title: Nothing reaches the runtime except through the gateway
body: The serving stack is not safe as an exposed edge service and its own API keys guard only part of the surface — so the gateway in front is mandatory, not optional: one governed door carrying workload identity per calling tenant, per-tenant quotas sized for finite capacity, and admission control that sheds load at the front rather than at the accelerator. The distributed control plane behind it — job APIs, inter-node channels — ships unauthenticated by design; network isolation is the control there, not a version bump. Assessment probe: enumerate every listening endpoint on the serving tier and demand the auth story for each.

items.title: A blocking promotion gate, and digest verification at load
body: Weights reach the runtime only through the promotion pipeline: format policy and scanning as a blocking gate, per-version evaluation because a new checkpoint is a new model, and a digest verified at load so the gate cannot be bypassed by writing to storage directly. Weights at rest get encryption, access control and integrity digests — the artifact is expensive to reproduce and trivial to copy.

items.title: Tenancy is a configuration review, not a default
body: Continuous batching mixes tenants in one forward pass; the KV and prefix caches hold their live context. Require tenant-scoped cache keys — published attacks reconstruct other tenants' prompts from cache-hit timing alone, so cross-tenant prefix sharing is off unless a review explicitly accepts it. For the highest-sensitivity tenants, hardware-backed isolation on the accelerators is the answer where shared silicon is not acceptable. Assessment probe: read the serving configuration and name which flags a tenant boundary depends on; anyone who cannot has not reviewed it.

items.title: Own the patch stream and the posture, including the gateway's
body: The serving stack is fast-moving third-party code with a live CVE stream, and nobody upstream patches it on your behalf — track it like any other exposed tier, and treat the gateway itself as supply chain: it is third-party code holding every tenant's credentials, an incident class with recent precedent. Posture management watches serving configuration for drift — versions, cache flags, bindings — and the guardrail checks a provider would have run are deployed at the gateway on both legs, because the output side is the half most often omitted.

items.title: Keep the lineage, the credentials and a privacy-conscious record
body: Three records this system cannot run honestly without. The artifact inventory: which model version is serving where, its publisher, format and the scan that cleared it — without it "what is running" has no answer. The credential story: storage pulls, registry reads and control-plane tokens issued short-lived from a secrets service, so the serving tier's environment holds nothing standing. And the request log from the gateway tap, kept privacy-consciously — the log of an inference service is itself a corpus of everything the organisation asked it.

items.title: Red-team every version, and promote in stages you can reverse
body: A new checkpoint from the same publisher is a new model nobody else has tested, and no provider is testing it on your behalf: adversarial evaluation runs per version, before promotion. Promotion itself is staged — a slice of traffic first, the previous version kept loadable — so rollback is a registry operation rather than a re-download under incident pressure.
